parsed.same_study_reason: Both lists describe a geo-randomized Facebook fundraising experiment for Save the Children across German postal codes. Both mention profitability/ROI, winsorizing at €1,000, spillovers to neighboring postal codes, competing charities, pre-registration and heterogeneity analyses.

pairs.reason: Both say the profitability/ROI conclusion rests on assumptions (behavioral assumptions vs. a lifetime-value multiplier) and wide uncertainty. Both ask that this uncertainty be shown more explicitly.
Both say the profitability conclusion is statistically fragile and should be stated more cautiously. B9 adds weak revenue significance and sensitivity to specification.

Both argue that the profitability/ROI estimates depend on winsorizing donations. A3 also covers the spillover estimate, while B4 is specific to the €1,000 cutoff and asks for alternative cutoffs and models.

Both say the neighbor-spillover estimate is unreliable. A3 blames arbitrary distance and functional-form assumptions; B8 notes the regression is non-randomized, so size and direction are uncertain. A3 also covers winsorizing.
Both say profitability conclusions depend on how the tails are handled (trimming/winsorizing). B9 states this generally, alongside specification and aggregation choices.
Both target the €1,000 winsorization. A4 objects that it departs from the pre-registered plan; B4 objects to its effect on inference given heavy tails.
Both mention normalizing effects per capita. A4 faults the departure from pre-registration, while B7 faults non-uniform ad exposure that makes per-capita effects hard to interpret.
Both concern effects on competing charities. A5 says the pre-registered analysis was omitted; B5 says the competitor data are incomplete and sector-wide giving is unobserved.
Both raise the length of the measurement window. A5 treats it vaguely as an analysis choice; B11 specifically worries about seasonal dynamics around the Dec 31 cutoff.
Both touch on heterogeneity analysis. A5 notes the pre-registered causal trees are missing; B2 raises multiplicity in exploratory subgroup interactions.
Both flag multiple-testing and false-positive risk in the heterogeneous-effect results. A7 adds implausible negative effects and missing F-tests.
Both involve covariate/pretreatment balance. A2 criticizes using hypothesis tests on balance tables, while B3 reports actual imbalance in alliance outcomes and possible residual confounding.
Both concern overstated claims relative to statistical evidence. A6 is generic about missing confidence intervals; B12 is about treating non-significant differences as equivalence.
Both concern claims stronger than the statistical uncertainty supports. A6 is generic about main results, while B9 targets weak revenue/ROI significance.
